lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Natural and Human Factors Influencing Climate Change

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify the natural factors that influence climate change.
- Describe ways of minimising human activities that influence climate change.
- Compare natural and human factors that influence climate change and green economy.

pages.title: What is Climate Change?
pages.body: Climate change refers to significant, long term shifts in global or regional weather patterns and average temperatures, distinct from the normal day to day or season to season variation in weather that occurs naturally. While Earth's climate has always changed gradually over very long time periods due to natural causes, the rapid changes observed over the past century are strongly linked to human activity, alongside ongoing natural influences.

questions.q: Climate change refers to
o: Normal daily weather variation only
Random, unpredictable events with no pattern
Short term seasonal changes only
Significant, long term shifts in weather patterns and temperatures
questions.e: Climate change refers to significant, long term shifts in global or regional weather patterns and average temperatures, distinct from the normal day to day or season to season variation in weather that occurs naturally.

pages.title: Natural Factors Influencing Climate Change
pages.body: Volcanic eruptions, which release ash and gases that can temporarily cool the atmosphere by blocking sunlight, variations in the Sun's energy output over long cycles, and natural, long term shifts in Earth's orbit and tilt, which affect how much solar energy different parts of the planet receive over thousands of years, are examples of natural factors that have influenced Earth's climate throughout its history, independent of human activity.

pages.title: Human Factors Influencing Climate Change
pages.body: Burning fossil fuels for energy, industry and transportation, deforestation, which reduces the number of trees available to absorb carbon (IV) oxide, and large scale livestock farming, which produces significant methane emissions, are major human activities that release greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, trapping additional heat and driving the rapid warming trend scientists have observed over the past century, well beyond what natural factors alone would explain.

pages.title: What is a Green Economy?
pages.body:
A green economy is an economic system designed to reduce environmental harm and resource depletion while still supporting human wellbeing and economic development, typically emphasising renewable energy, resource efficiency, and sustainable practices across industry, agriculture and daily life. Building a green economy is closely connected to addressing climate change, since many of the same actions that reduce environmental harm, such as shifting to renewable energy, also directly reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

[[pic:A two column comparison chart, one column headed Natural Factors showing small icons for a volcanic eruption, the Sun, and Earth's orbit, and the other column headed Human Factors showing small icons for a factory chimney, a deforested area, and cattle, with a shared arrow from both columns pointing down to a single label reading Climate Change, showing both categories contribute to the same overall effect.]]

Notice that while both natural and human factors influence climate, scientific evidence strongly indicates that the current rapid pace of warming is driven predominantly by human factors, since natural factors alone cannot account for the scale and speed of recent changes observed.

pages.title: Ways of Minimising Human Activities That Influence Climate Change
pages.body: Shifting toward renewable energy sources such as solar and wind power, reducing deforestation and actively planting new trees, improving energy efficiency in homes, industry and transportation, and adopting more sustainable farming practices are key strategies for minimising the human factors contributing to climate change. Many of these strategies directly connect to the energy conservation and conversion topics studied in an earlier strand, showing how different areas of science and daily life connect to this shared global challenge.

pages.title: Comparing Natural and Human Factors
pages.body: Timescale, controllability, and current significance are useful points of comparison between natural and human factors influencing climate change. Natural factors typically operate over very long timescales, from years for volcanic effects to thousands of years for orbital changes, and are essentially uncontrollable by human action. Human factors, by contrast, have developed rapidly over just the past two centuries, are directly linked to specific, identifiable human choices and activities, and are therefore, at least in principle, controllable through changed behaviour, policy and technology, which is precisely why current climate action efforts focus so heavily on addressing human factors specifically.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

International scientific bodies, such as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, continuously study and report on the relative contributions of natural and human factors to climate change, consistently concluding that human activity, particularly the burning of fossil fuels, is the dominant driver of the rapid warming observed since the industrial era began.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Researching Climate Change and Green Economy Actions

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Research into climate change and green economy actions in Ghana.
- Access climate change and green economy actions in other countries.

pages.title: Why Research Climate Actions?
pages.body: Understanding what specific actions Ghana and other countries are actually taking to address climate change and support a green economy, rather than relying only on general awareness that these are global concerns, allows for a more informed, evidence based understanding of current progress, remaining challenges, and realistic opportunities for further action.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Climate Change and Green Economy Actions in Ghana

pages.title: Climate Change and Green Economy Actions in Ghana
pages.body: Ghana has pursued several notable climate and green economy actions, including expanding solar power generation capacity, promoting afforestation and reforestation programmes to restore tree cover lost to deforestation, and developing national policies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions in line with international climate agreements. Ghana has also taken steps to address illegal small scale mining, known as galamsey, studied in an earlier strand, recognising its significant environmental impact, alongside broader efforts to improve waste management, studied earlier in this strand, which also connects to reducing methane emissions from decomposing organic waste.

pages.title: Researching Ghana's Climate Actions
pages.body: Reliable sources for researching Ghana's climate change and green economy actions include official government agency publications, such as those from the Environmental Protection Agency, reports from international organisations that track national climate commitments, and reputable national and international news coverage of specific government policies and programmes. When conducting this research, it is useful to look specifically for concrete, named actions and programmes, rather than only general statements of intent, since specific actions are easier to evaluate for genuine effectiveness.

lessons.title: Climate Change and Green Economy Actions in Other Countries

pages.title: Climate Change and Green Economy Actions in Other Countries
pages.body:
Different countries have pursued a wide variety of climate and green economy strategies suited to their own particular circumstances, resources and priorities. Some countries have invested heavily in large scale renewable energy infrastructure, such as extensive wind farms or solar installations. Others have introduced strong policy measures, such as carbon pricing, which places a financial cost on greenhouse gas emissions, encouraging businesses and individuals to reduce their emissions. Still others have focused heavily on reforestation and habitat protection, or on transforming transportation systems to reduce reliance on fossil fuel powered vehicles.

[[pic:A world map style infographic with Ghana highlighted and labelled with icons representing solar power expansion, afforestation, and galamsey enforcement, alongside two or three other countries highlighted with different icons representing their own distinct climate actions, such as wind farms, carbon pricing, or electric vehicle policy, with a shared legend explaining each icon.]]

Notice how different countries, including Ghana, pursue climate and green economy actions suited to their own specific resources, geography and economic priorities, rather than following a single, identical global approach.

pages.title: Accessing and Evaluating Climate Data Responsibly
pages.body: When accessing information about climate change and green economy actions in other countries, it is important to consult credible, well established sources, such as official government publications, recognised international organisations, and peer reviewed research, rather than relying on unverified social media claims or sources with a clear bias that might exaggerate or understate genuine progress. Comparing information from multiple credible sources helps build a more balanced, accurate picture of what different countries are genuinely achieving.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Examples of Climate Change and Green Economy Actions in Ghana and Other Countries

pages.title: Examples of Climate Change and Green Economy Actions in Ghana and Other Countries
pages.body:
| **COUNTRY** | **ACTION** | **WHAT IT ACHIEVES** |
|---|---|---|
| **Ghana** | Green Ghana Day, an annual national tree planting exercise that began in 2021. Promotion of solar power, improved cookstoves and the recycling of plastics | Restores forest cover, reduces the use of firewood and charcoal and creates green jobs |
| **Kenya** | A ban on plastic carrier bags since 2017. Most of its electricity comes from geothermal, hydro and wind power | Less plastic pollution and low emissions from electricity |
| **Rwanda** | A ban on plastic bags since 2008 and a monthly community clean up day | Clean cities and strong public participation |
| **Morocco** | The Noor solar power complex near Ouarzazate, one of the largest solar power stations of its kind in the world | Clean electricity for a large number of homes and less imported fuel |
| **Ethiopia** | The Green Legacy programme of mass tree planting | Billions of seedlings planted to restore land and reduce erosion |
| **Costa Rica** | Almost all its electricity comes from renewable sources, and landowners are paid to protect forests | Forest cover has increased greatly and emissions from electricity are very low |
| **Germany** | A long term plan to replace coal and nuclear power with wind and solar power, and a deposit scheme for returning bottles | A large and growing share of renewable electricity and high recycling rates |
| **China** | The largest producer and installer of solar panels and wind turbines, and the largest market for electric vehicles | Lower cost of clean technology for the whole world |

Almost all countries have signed the Paris Agreement of 2015, in which they agreed to keep the rise in the average temperature of the Earth well below 2 degrees Celsius and to try to limit it to 1.5 degrees Celsius. Each country writes its own plan of action and reports its progress.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

International climate agreements, such as the Paris Agreement, provide a useful, shared reference framework against which individual countries' climate actions, including Ghana's, can be meaningfully compared, since most countries that are party to such agreements report on their progress using broadly similar reporting standards, making cross country research and comparison considerably more straightforward than it would otherwise be.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Compare and contrast climate change and green economy actions in Ghana and other countries.
- Identify and write the effective initiatives that address climate change and green economy issues in Ghana and other countries.
- Prescribe, with reasons, best practices to serve as possible solutions to address climate change and green economy issues in Ghana.

pages.title: Building on Prior Research
pages.body: Having researched specific climate change and green economy actions in Ghana and other countries in Lesson 11, this lesson focuses on comparing that information critically, identifying which initiatives appear genuinely effective, and using that evidence to recommend realistic best practices suited to Ghana's specific circumstances.

pages.title: Comparing Climate Actions Across Countries
pages.body: Scale of investment, policy strength, public participation, and measurable results are useful criteria for comparing and contrasting climate change and green economy actions between Ghana and other countries. A country investing heavily in renewable energy infrastructure with strong supporting policy and high public participation would generally be expected to show more measurable progress than a country with only limited investment or weak policy enforcement, even if both have officially stated similar climate goals.

pages.title: Identifying Genuinely Effective Initiatives
pages.body:
An effective climate or green economy initiative is one that produces measurable, verifiable results, such as a documented reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, a significant increase in renewable energy capacity, or a measurable increase in forest cover, rather than an initiative that exists only as an announced policy with little evidence of real world impact. Identifying such initiatives requires looking beyond stated intentions to actual reported outcomes and data, as emphasised in the research approach studied in Lesson 11.

[[pic:A simple comparison table style diagram with column headers reading Country, Key Initiative, and Measurable Result, showing three example rows, Ghana with an afforestation programme and a stated area of forest restored, and two other countries each with a different initiative and its own measurable result, allowing direct visual comparison of initiative type and effectiveness across countries.]]

Notice how presenting climate initiatives alongside their measurable results, rather than simply listing initiative names, allows a much more meaningful, evidence based comparison between countries.

pages.title: Prescribing Best Practices for Ghana
pages.body: Drawing on genuinely effective initiatives identified both within Ghana and internationally, best practices can be recommended for Ghana's specific context, taking into account the country's available resources, existing infrastructure, and particular environmental challenges, such as galamsey and deforestation, studied earlier. For example, if solar power expansion has proven effective both in Ghana and in other countries with strong sunshine, continuing to invest in and expand this initiative would be a reasonable, evidence supported recommendation. Similarly, if stronger enforcement against illegal mining has proven effective at reducing environmental damage elsewhere, strengthening similar enforcement mechanisms in Ghana would be a well justified recommendation.

pages.title: Justifying Recommendations with Reasons
pages.body: Any recommended best practice should be accompanied by clear reasoning, explaining specifically why that particular practice is expected to work well in Ghana's context, ideally supported by evidence of it working effectively elsewhere or already showing promising results within Ghana itself. A recommendation without supporting reasoning is far less convincing and useful than one grounded in specific, comparable evidence.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Government policy makers, researchers and international development organisations routinely carry out this same type of comparative analysis, studying which climate and green economy initiatives have proven effective in similar contexts elsewhere, before recommending or adapting them for a specific country's own circumstances, meaning the analytical skill practised in this lesson mirrors real, professional policy analysis work.
